body:
What Are the Fruits That We Bring?

Bikkurim and Belonging · The Journey Behind the Fruit · Bracha and Klalah · Kumi Ori

I. Coming Home

A week and a half ago, coming home from my longest trip to Chutz La'aretz since making aliyah, something happened that was not expected. The emotion did not arrive at baggage claim or at the front door. It arrived the moment the plane touched down in Eretz Yisrael.

On the verge of tears. Three weeks away. It was painful.

There is something about this Land that does not let go, that pulls at something deeper than geography or habit. Baruch Hashem, the family returned shortly afterward from the remainder of their trip abroad. This week, the children started school. Life resumed its rhythm.

And now, reading this week's parsha, those words hit differently:

והיה כי תבוא אל הארץ אשר ה׳ אלקיך נתן לך נחלה וירשתה וישבת בה

"When you come into the Land that Hashem your God gives you as an inheritance, and you possess it and settle in it."

— Devarim 26:1

Ki savo el ha'aretz. When you come into the Land.

The Torah does not stop with coming. There is virishtah, possessing it. Then v'yashavta bah, settling in it. And then something has to grow.

II. What Bikkurim Asks of Us

Ki Savo begins with Bikkurim, one of those mitzvos whose very existence is inseparable from Eretz Yisrael. There are mitzvos that can only be performed in the Land and others which didn’t go into effect until after we first arrived. We saw something similar earlier in the Torah: after the punishment of the Meraglim, the Torah immediately spoke about mitzvos connected to entering Eretz Yisrael, including hafrashat challah. The pattern is consistent. Certain obligations only come alive when we arrive and other when we are still inside.

Bikkurim is a remarkable mitzvah. It is tempting to call it "cool," which is not a word typically applied to mitzvos, but there is something so impactful about what it represents. It connects directly to the reality that a person has come into Eretz Yisrael, received it as an inheritance, possessed it, and settled it.

We live in a world that builds quickly. High tech can produce something functional in minutes. Even physical construction has become astonishingly fast. But Bikkurim cannot be manufactured overnight. The land has to produce it. There are agricultural halachos governing the process: orlah, neta revai. Time passes. Trees grow. Seasons turn. Eventually there comes the moment when a person can identify those first fruits that qualify as Bikkurim.

That means something has not just taken root but also produced fruits themselves. That means settlement is real.

III. Your Fruit Did Not Begin With You

And then the Torah does something surprising. When a person finally stands holding the fruit of his own land and his own labor, the Torah does not have him say, "Look what I grew." Instead, it tells him to speak about his history.

ארמי אבד אבי

"An Aramean sought to destroy my father."

— Devarim 26:5

The farmer speaks about Yaakov Avinu. The descent to Mitzrayim. Becoming a nation there. Slavery and oppression. Crying out to Hashem. Hashem taking us out with a strong hand and an outstretched arm. And finally, Hashem bringing us into Eretz Yisrael and giving us this Land, a land flowing with milk and honey. Only after recounting all of that can he say:

ועתה הנה הבאתי את ראשית פרי האדמה אשר נתתה לי ה׳

"And now, behold, I have brought the first fruit of the land that You have given me, Hashem."

— Devarim 26:10

The fruit in a person's hand did not begin when he noticed it growing on the tree. There was a tree before there was fruit. There was planting before there was a tree. There was land before there was planting. There was conquest and settlement before that land became his. Forty years in the Midbar before that. Yetzias Mitzrayim before that. Slavery before that. The Avos before that. A promise from Hashem before any of it.

Life does not occur in a vacuum. There are so many moments, so many interactions, so many stages that bring us, step by step, until we reach the moment we are standing in today. Mikra Bikkurim defines that. We have the joy of bringing our first fruits. We get to share from the wealth of our inheritance, from what Hashem has given us. But the Torah insists that we remember why we are able to do so. We are a Jew with land in Eretz Yisrael, with fruit growing from that land. We have been able to build something. The proper response is not pride in the fruit alone. It is awe at the journey that made the fruit possible.

IV. What We Receive Does Not End With Us

From Bikkurim, the parsha moves directly into Vidui Maaser. Who are we giving to? The Levi, the ger, the orphan, the widow. What Hashem gives us does not terminate with us. There are obligations created by what we receive.

This is a quietly powerful transition. Bikkurim is about recognizing where our blessings came from. Vidui Maaser is about recognizing where they need to go. The fruit does not exist only for the one who grew it. It has a purpose beyond the farmer's table. And the same is true of everything Hashem gives us: our talents, our resources, our Torah, our capacity to build. None of it ends with us. All of it carries an obligation outward.

V. Stones, an Altar, and a Question

The parsha then moves into another fascinating section. After crossing the Yarden, Bnei Yisrael are commanded to erect stones, write the Torah upon them, and build an altar on Har Eival. There are other places in Torah where we are very careful about where and how korbanos can be offered. Eventually, avodah becomes centralized in the place Hashem chooses, ultimately the Beis HaMikdash. Yet here Hashem specifically commands this altar on Har Eival as part of the entry into the Land.

And then comes the ceremony of brachah and klalah, introduced earlier in Parashas Re'eh and now described in full. One of the declarations:

ארור האיש אשר יעשה פסל ומסכה

"Cursed is the man who makes an idol or molten image."

— Devarim 27:15

Chazal explain that the corresponding bracha was also declared:

ברוך האיש אשר לא יעשה פסל ומסכה

"Blessed is the man who does not make an idol or molten image."

There is an important distinction sitting inside this juxtaposition. Hashem told us to build the stones and the altar. Hashem did not tell us to build an idol. The question is not simply, "Am I building something?" The question is: "Am I doing what Hashem wants me to be doing?"

The klalot themselves are not punishments waiting to be imposed. They are warnings given precisely because Hashem wants us to receive the brachah. He gives us the framework. He shows us the road. He wants us to succeed.

VI. The Tools of Success

This connects beautifully to last week's parsha, Ki Seitzei. The Gemara records the opinion that a ben sorer u'moreh never actually occurred and never will occur. Why, then, is it written?

דרוש וקבל שכר

"Study it and receive reward."

— Sanhedrin 71a

The Torah gives us knowledge. It gives us boundaries. It shows us consequences before we reach them. Hashem wants us to be able to bring our Bikkurim. He wants us to be proud of where we came from, where we are going, who we were, and what we are becoming. The tools of success are all there.

What do we have to do? We learn, and we do. Na'aseh v'nishma. Sometimes avodas Hashem means sitting deeply in our sefarim. But sometimes it means planting the field. Sometimes it means growing the trees. Because if we do not grow the fruit, we do not get to bring the fruit. And we do not get to stand there and recite Mikra Bikkurim, reminding ourselves of everything that had to happen for us to be zocheh to this extraordinary gift.

VII. The Joy and the Cost

Chazal describe the processions of those who brought Bikkurim to Yerushalayim, and they are magnificent. There was music. People came out to greet the procession. The wealthy brought their fruits in baskets of silver and gold, while others brought them in woven baskets.

There is tremendous simcha in Bikkurim. And yet there is also something it asks of us. We leave our fields behind. We travel to Yerushalayim. The mitzvah requires something, not just celebration but effort and sacrifice. There is so often a plus and a minus to things in life.

But when everything is done b'derech kedushah, according to what Hashem actually asks of us, then even actions that might look identical from the outside can be entirely different from the inside. The altar on Har Eival is not an idol. The stones bearing Torah are not monuments to human ego. The journey to Yerushalayim is not a burden but an expression of belonging. What makes the difference is whether we are doing what Hashem asked us to do.

VIII. So What Is In Bikkurim For Me?

Bikkurim is not a mitzvah that most of us can perform today in its actual form. Even when the Beis HaMikdash stands, not every Jew owns agricultural land. There are 613 mitzvos, but no individual Jew can personally perform all 613. Not everyone is a Kohen. Not everyone is a Levi. There are mitzvos whose circumstances simply do not apply to every person.

So what is in Bikkurim for us?

On one level, Chazal teach the enormous value of learning Torah even when a particular mitzvah cannot presently be performed.

But there is also something deeply personal here. Coming home to Eretz Yisrael after weeks abroad, ki savo el ha'aretz feels less like a pasuk and more like a lived experience. And the Torah does not stop at arrival. Virishtah v'yashavta bah. Possess it and settle in it. That first week home, while the family was still abroad, the apartment did not feel complete. There was definitely less stress in certain areas of life, but it did not feel like settling. It felt almost like being a passerby who happened to have an apartment and bills to pay.

Then the family came home.

And suddenly: v'yashavta bah.

Now there was settling.

IX. Zera

There is an image that will not let go.

The Hebrew word for children, for offspring, is zera. The same language as seed, as planting. Our children are the fruits we get to raise. They are obviously not Bikkurim in the halachic sense. But the image speaks powerfully.

These are the fruits of our labor, the lives we cultivate and nurture. No matter what, these are our children. Our gift. Our gift to Hashem and to Klal Yisrael.

They drive us nuts.

We love them.

Both statements are absolutely true. They are our pride and joy, and that expression is not a cliché. It is real.

But what makes them ours? Go back through Mikra Bikkurim. Arami oved avi. Our ancestors went down to Mitzrayim. We became a nation. We were oppressed. We cried out to Hashem. And then, as we speak about every Pesach, Hashem took us out with a strong hand and an outstretched arm. And eventually we arrived in Eretz Yisrael.

For someone who experienced the joys of marriage and children a little later in life, after already being here in Eretz Yisrael, the Land became, in an especially personal way, the land flowing with milk and honey. And then the fruits appear. Baruch Hashem.

X. Kumi Ori: The Tochacha Reversed

This week's haftarah follows the devastating Tochacha of Ki Savo with one of the most extraordinary descriptions of restoration in all of Tanach. It opens:

קומי אורי כי בא אורך וכבוד ה׳ עליך זרח

"Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of Hashem has shone upon you."

— Yeshayahu 60:1

And then:

כי הנה החשך יכסה ארץ וערפל לאמים ועליך יזרח ה׳ וכבודו עליך יראה

"For behold, darkness shall cover the earth and thick darkness the nations, but Hashem will shine upon you, and His glory will be seen upon you."

— Yeshayahu 60:2

It is literally light. And from there it is bracha after bracha. The children come home. The nations come toward Yerushalayim. The walls are rebuilt. The gates are opened. Those who oppressed us bow before Tzion. Instead of being uprooted from the Land, l'olam yirshu aretz, we inherit the Land forever. Instead of being scattered among the nations, kulam nikbetzu va'u lach, they all gather and return. Instead of ein moshi'a, there being no savior, Hashem says:

וידעת כי אני ה׳ מושיעך וגאלך

"You will know that I am Hashem, your Savior and your Redeemer."

— Yeshayahu 60:16

Everything we went through gets to bring us toward where we are going.

XI. What Are My Bikkurim?

We are now deep into Chodesh Elul, and Elul is an especially meaningful month. It contains so many family milestones, both simcha and loss. Marriage and growth. Mourning for fellow Yidden who helped bring us to where we are today. Birth: our own, our parents', our children's. And through all of those stages, we get to have these extraordinary zechuyos in Eretz Yisrael.

The farmer stands in Yerushalayim. He looks down at his basket. He sees a fruit. But the Torah tells him to see thousands of years.

Perhaps that is part of our cheshbon hanefesh as well. We look at where we are today and ask: how did we get here? Who brought us here? What did Hashem give us? What did we do with it?

And most importantly: what are our Bikkurim?

Besides our children, what have we planted? What fruits are growing? What are we harvesting that we can bring and share with Klal Yisrael? And how can we do it better? How can we do so much more?

Hashem gives us the Land. Hashem gives us the seed. Hashem gives us the Torah. Hashem gives us the bracha and shows us the road that leads toward it. But we still have to plant. We still have to grow. And, Baruch Hashem, we get to bring the fruits.

חזק ואחזק

Good Shabbos, and a Shanah Tovah u’Metukah.

Reflection Questions

• What are my Bikkurim? What have I planted, cultivated, and grown that I can bring before Hashem and share with Klal Yisrael?

• When I look at the blessings in my life, do I see only the fruit, or can I trace the journey that made the fruit possible?

• Where in my life is what Hashem has given me terminating with me, rather than flowing outward to the Levi, the ger, the orphan, and the widow?

• Am I building what Hashem wants me to build, or am I building something that looks impressive from the outside but was never asked of me?

• Is there an area of my life where I am still a passerby rather than truly settled, and what would it take to move from virishtah to v'yashavta bah?

• What can I plant now, during Elul, so that next year's Bikkurim are even greater?
